parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A woman phones a company to hire a car.
script: Good morning, Sunway Car Hire, Carlos speaking.
Hello, I'd like to hire a car for my holiday next month.
Certainly. Could I have your name?
Joyce Hartley. H, A, R, T, L, E, Y.
Thank you, Mrs Hartley. When would you like to pick up the car?
And where would you like to collect it?
At the airport. We land at the North terminal, not the South one.
No problem. What size of car do you need?
I was thinking of a small one, but we'll have two large suitcases, so probably a medium-sized car.
Automatic, please. I'm not used to driving a manual car.
And how long will you need it?
A medium automatic is thirty-eight pounds a day. That includes basic insurance.
That's fine. Can we have a child seat? Our son is four.
Yes, there's no extra charge for that. Will anyone else be driving?
Yes, my husband will share the driving.
I'll add him as an additional driver. Finally, please remember that the car must be returned with a full tank of petrol, otherwise there's a refuelling charge.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A guide introduces a heritage walking trail in an old town.
script: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to the Old Harbour Heritage Trail. I'm Maria, and I'll be your guide today.
The trail was created five years ago by the local history society. The council paid for the signs, but all the research was done by volunteers.
The full trail takes about two hours, including stops. Some people try to do it in one hour, but then you miss most of the stories.
Many of the streets are cobbled, and they can be slippery, so I hope you're all wearing comfortable shoes.
We'll finish at the river, where there's a café if you'd like to relax afterwards.

Let me tell you about some of the places we'll see. Our first stop is the clock tower. It's not especially old, but you can climb to the top, and from there you get a wonderful view over the whole harbour.
Next is the old courthouse. The cells in the basement were used as the town prison until the eighteen-nineties, and you can still see the prisoners' names carved into the walls.
Then we'll visit the merchant's house, which is famous for its painted ceilings. They're the original seventeenth-century paintings, and they were only discovered during repairs in 1985.
After that is the covered market. It's still a working market, and the stalls sell local cheese, bread and fish, so it's a good place to pick up some lunch.
Then there's the chapel. You'll see scaffolding around it at the moment, because it's being restored after storm damage.
And finally, the customs house. It's a beautiful building, but it's privately owned and closed to the public, so we'll only see it from outside.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two biology students, Liam and Chloe, plan an experiment on light and plant growth.
script: Chloe, why did you want to do an experiment on light colour and plant growth?
I read an article about vertical farms that use pink light, and I wondered whether different colours really make a difference.
OK. Which plant should we use? I suggested beans.
Beans are too slow for our timetable. Cress grows very quickly, so we'll get results in two weeks.
Fair enough. When we did the trial run, what was the main problem?
Light was leaking between the sections, so the plants weren't really getting just one colour.
I was going to measure height, but tall plants aren't necessarily healthier. I think dry mass is a better measure. We dry the plants and weigh them.
And how should we present the results?
A bar chart, with one bar for each colour. That makes the comparison really clear.
Let's go through the method. First we divide the box into four sections.
Using pieces of cardboard, sealed with tape this time so no light gets through.
Then each section gets a different coloured bulb: red, blue, green and white.
In each pot we plant twenty seeds.
Ten millilitres every morning, so every pot gets exactly the same.
And we take the measurements after fourteen days.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecture on the history of glass.
script: Good morning. Today's lecture is about a material that surrounds us but that we rarely think about: glass.
Glass is made by heating a mixture of sand, soda and lime to a very high temperature until it melts. When it cools, it becomes hard but remains transparent.
The earliest known glass objects are beads from Mesopotamia, made around four thousand five hundred years ago. For centuries, glass was rare and valuable.

The great breakthrough came in the first century BC, when craftsmen in the Roman world invented glass blowing. This made it possible to produce glass vessels quickly and cheaply, and glass became part of everyday life.

In the Middle Ages, Venice became the centre of European glassmaking. In 1291, the city ordered all glassmakers to move to the nearby island of Murano, partly because of the risk of fire in a city of wooden buildings. The glassmakers were highly respected, but they were forbidden to leave, so that their secrets would not spread.

Modern window glass owes a great deal to Alastair Pilkington, who in the 1950s developed the float glass process. Molten glass is poured onto a bath of molten tin, where it spreads out to form a perfectly flat sheet.

Today, glass has uses its inventors could never have imagined. Fibre optic cables, made of extremely thin strands of glass, carry most of the world's internet data. And the screens on our smartphones are made of specially toughened glass that resists scratches.

Finally, glass is excellent for the environment in one respect: it can be recycled again and again without losing quality. Recycling also saves energy, because broken glass melts at a lower temperature than raw materials.

passages.title: Saving the Kiwi
paragraphs: The kiwi is New Zealand's national symbol, so closely identified with the country that New Zealanders themselves are often called 'Kiwis'. Yet this unusual bird is under serious threat. There are five species, all of them flightless and most of them active only at night. Of an estimated twelve million kiwi in New Zealand before humans arrived, fewer than 70,000 remain.

The kiwi is unlike any other bird. It is one of several flightless birds in New Zealand, a country that had no land mammals apart from bats before humans arrived, so birds took over many roles that mammals play elsewhere. The kiwi's nostrils are at the tip of its long beak, and it finds worms and insects mainly by smell, which is unusual among birds. Females lay one of the largest eggs relative to body size of any bird, weighing around a fifth of the mother's body weight.

The main threat today comes from introduced predators. Stoats, small relatives of the weasel, were brought to New Zealand in the 1880s to control rabbits, which had themselves been introduced and become a pest. Instead, the stoats found easier prey among native birds. Together with cats, dogs and other introduced animals, they have devastated kiwi populations. In areas without predator control, around 95 percent of kiwi chicks die before reaching adulthood, most of them killed by stoats and cats.

Conservationists have responded in several ways. One of the most successful programmes, Operation Nest Egg, was launched in 1994 by a partnership of conservation organisations. Eggs are taken from nests in the wild and hatched in hatcheries. The chicks are then raised in safe conditions until they weigh about one kilogram, when they are large enough to defend themselves against stoats, and returned to the wild.

Local communities also play a major role. Across the country, volunteers set and check thousands of traps to catch stoats, rats and other predators, often on land near their own homes. In areas where trapping is intensive, kiwi numbers have begun to rise.

In 2016, the New Zealand government announced an even more ambitious goal: to eliminate stoats, rats and possums from the entire country by 2050. Supporters argue that new technologies, such as smarter traps and genetic methods, could make this possible. Many scientists, however, question whether the target can be achieved, given the size of the task and the cost involved.

passages.title: Working Less, Achieving More?
paragraphs: For most of the past century, the standard working week in many countries has been five days. Recently, however, a growing number of organisations have experimented with a four-day week. Most trials follow what is called the 100-80-100 model: employees receive 100 percent of their pay for working 80 percent of their previous hours, in exchange for maintaining 100 percent of their productivity.

Some of the earliest large-scale trials took place in Iceland between 2015 and 2019. Around 2,500 public sector workers, including office staff, nurses and police officers, reduced their hours from 40 to 35 or 36 a week without a cut in pay. Researchers found that productivity was maintained or improved in most workplaces, and that workers reported less stress. Following the trials, unions negotiated new agreements, and a large majority of Iceland's workforce now has the right to shorter hours.

In 2022, the largest trial so far was organised in the United Kingdom, involving 61 companies and around 2,900 employees. After six months, 56 of the companies decided to continue with the four-day week, and 18 made it permanent. Employees reported significantly lower levels of burnout and better sleep, while company revenues remained broadly stable.

How can people do the same amount of work in less time? Companies taking part in trials often redesigned the way they worked. Many cut the length and number of meetings, introduced periods when staff could work without interruption, and reduced time spent on unnecessary emails. In effect, the shorter week forced organisations to identify and remove activities that added little value.

The four-day week is not without its critics. It is far easier to introduce in offices than in sectors such as healthcare, retail or manufacturing, where work is tied to opening hours or production lines. Some workers who have moved to compressed hours, working the same total hours over four longer days, report feeling more tired, not less. Critics also argue that the model is harder for small businesses, which have fewer staff to cover absences.

Interest nevertheless continues to grow. In 2019, Microsoft Japan reported a 40 percent rise in productivity during a month-long trial, although the experiment was short and the results have been questioned. In 2022, Belgium gave workers the legal right to request to work their full hours over four days instead of five. Whether the four-day week becomes the new standard remains to be seen, but the evidence so far suggests it can work well in the right conditions.

passages.title: Do Animals Have Feelings?
paragraphs: In 1872 Charles Darwin published The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals, in which he argued that many animals experience emotions such as fear, anger and joy, and express them in ways similar to humans. For much of the following century, however, his ideas were largely ignored by scientists. The dominant school of psychology, behaviourism, held that only observable behaviour could be studied scientifically, and that talk of animals' inner feelings was unscientific speculation.

In my view, the behaviourists were wrong to dismiss animal emotions so completely. Over recent decades, researchers have found ways to study emotions in animals without simply guessing what they feel. The neuroscientist Jaak Panksepp, for example, discovered that rats produce high-pitched sounds, too high for human ears, when they are tickled, and that they actively seek out the hand that tickles them. He argued that these sounds were a form of laughter, reflecting a basic emotional system shared by many mammals.

Other studies have explored more complex responses. In a famous experiment, the primatologists Sarah Brosnan and Frans de Waal trained capuchin monkeys to exchange small stones for food. When both monkeys in a pair received pieces of cucumber, they were content. But when one monkey saw its partner receive grapes, a more desirable reward, for the same task, it often refused its cucumber, sometimes throwing it away. This suggests a sensitivity to unfair treatment, although it would be a mistake to assume the monkeys understand fairness exactly as humans do.

Evidence of emotional states has even been found in insects. In one study, honeybees that had been shaken vigorously, to simulate an attack, responded to ambiguous smells as if they expected something bad, a pattern that researchers described as pessimistic. Elephants, meanwhile, have been observed returning to the bones of dead relatives and touching them with their trunks, behaviour that many researchers interpret as a form of mourning.

In 2012 a group of prominent neuroscientists signed the Cambridge Declaration on Consciousness, which stated that many animals, including all mammals and birds, possess the brain structures needed for conscious experience. There are, of course, real dangers in anthropomorphism, the tendency to assume that animals feel exactly as we do. A dog that looks 'guilty' may simply be reacting to its owner's angry voice. But I believe that refusing to recognise any emotions in animals is an equally serious error.

These questions have practical consequences. If animals can suffer, then how we farm, transport and experiment on them becomes a moral issue. In 2022 the United Kingdom passed a law recognising animals as sentient beings, and following a scientific review, it included octopuses, crabs and lobsters. In my view, the growing scientific evidence on animal emotions should shape how we treat the animals in our care.

task1.text: The bar chart below shows the percentage of men and women in four age groups who exercised regularly in one country in 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
model: The bar chart compares the proportion of men and women in four age groups who took regular exercise in one country in 2024.
Overall, regular exercise became less common with age for both sexes. Men were more active than women in the younger age groups, but this pattern was reversed among people aged 45 and over.

Among 18 to 29-year-olds, 58% of men exercised regularly, compared with half of women, the largest gap between the sexes in any age group. In the 30 to 44 age group, the figures were much closer, at 46% for men and 44% for women.

From the age of 45, women were more likely to exercise than men. In the 45 to 59 group, 41% of women exercised regularly, slightly higher than the figure of 38% for men. Among people aged 60 and over, the proportions fell to their lowest levels, with 35% of women and only 30% of men taking regular exercise.

task2.text: Some people think governments should spend money on exploring outer space. Others believe this money should be spent on solving problems on Earth. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write at least 250 words.
model: Space exploration costs governments billions of dollars every year, and many people question whether this is a sensible use of public money. Although I understand the argument for focusing on problems at home, I believe that a moderate level of investment in space research is justified.

Those who oppose space spending argue that there are more urgent needs. Millions of people lack clean water, healthcare and education, and climate change threatens communities around the world. From this point of view, sending robots to Mars while people go hungry seems hard to justify. Moreover, private companies are now investing heavily in space, so some argue that governments no longer need to.

On the other hand, space research has brought enormous practical benefits. Satellites allow us to forecast the weather, monitor crops and forests, and track the effects of climate change, while technologies developed for space missions have led to improvements in medical imaging, water purification and materials. In addition, space programmes inspire young people to study science and engineering, which benefits the wider economy. It is also worth noting that space budgets are small compared with spending on health or defence; NASA's budget, for example, is well under one percent of US government spending.

In my view, the choice is not as simple as space or Earth. Much space research directly helps us understand and protect our own planet. Governments should continue to fund it, but should prioritise missions with clear scientific or practical value, such as Earth observation, over prestige projects.
In conclusion, while problems on Earth must remain the main priority, I believe that carefully targeted spending on space exploration is a worthwhile investment in our future.

speaking.cue:
Describe a time when you helped someone.
You should say:
- who you helped
- what the situation was
- how you helped them
and explain how you felt about it.
speaking.cueModel: I'd like to talk about a time last year when I helped a first-year student at my university. I was in the library one evening, and I noticed a girl sitting near me who looked really stressed. She kept typing and deleting things, and eventually I asked if she was OK. It turned out she had a programming assignment due at midnight, and her code wouldn't run. She'd only just started university and had never programmed before, so she was close to tears. I'd done exactly the same course the previous year, so I sat down with her and we went through the code line by line. The problem turned out to be quite small, just a missing bracket and a variable with the wrong name, but she'd been stuck on it for hours. Rather than just fixing it for her, I tried to explain how to read the error messages, so she could solve similar problems herself. She submitted the assignment with about half an hour to spare. I felt really good afterwards, partly because I remembered how lost I'd felt in my first year. We're actually friends now, and she sometimes asks me for advice about her courses.
